utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The proceedings this morning have been set aside for submissions under Rule 98 bis. We begin first with submissions on behalf of Mr. Sikirica. Mr. Greaves. I should remind you that the time of approximately 45 minutes has been allocated for each submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for the transcript to appear, Your Honours. Your Honours, can I first of all deal with matters which arise from concessions made by the Prosecution in their reply concerning Dusko Sikirica. They make a concession in respect of counts 1 and 2, and looking at counts 1 and 2, they formally charge him at page 9 of the indictment under both Article 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute in relation to genocide and complicity to commit genocide. It follows from their concession that in respect of that part of each count, we submit that those two items should be deleted from each count. There is, secondly, a concession in respect of counts 12 to 15, which are set out at page 14 of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I must interrupt. The concession relates to 7(3), as I recollect; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not plain.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Article 7(3). I think I said that, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You didn't, but no matter. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I apologise. I should have made it plain. I thought I had. It's in respect of Article 7(3) only. The second matter in respect of which there is a concession relates to counts 12 to 15, which are set out at pages 14 and 15 of the English language version of the indictment. The concession there - and I'm looking at paragraph 14 of the Prosecution's response - the Prosecution acknowledges that the accused should be acquitted with respect to liability for those offences, counts 12 to 13, because those two are allegations of torture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Greaves --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I can overhear Your Honour. I was about to bring you to the paragraph which charges this defendant with responsibility for that. Can I ask you to look at paragraph 14, please, and paragraph 17. Those are the two general allegations which deal with torture. Looking at the two counts themselves, Damir Dosen and Dusko Knezevic are alleged to have committed the offences, but by virtue of paragraph 17, Sikirica is charged with superior authority, responsibility in respect of those matters, as I understand it. And I take it from the Prosecution's concessions that are made that it's in that way and under that paragraph, and I see my learned friend Mr. Mundis nodding, and I'm grateful to him for so doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm not following this. It's not plain. Are you saying that your client is, although not named in counts 12 to 15, in some way charged under those counts?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. If Your Honour looks at paragraph 17, please: "In addition, Dusko Sikirica is also, or alternatively, criminally responsible for acts of subordinates with respect to the crimes charged in the Indictment..." Counts 12 and 13 are charged in the indictment, and the Prosecution's concession is a failure to adduce sufficient evidence that would satisfy all the elements of these charges, sets out in its footnote to paragraph 14, footnote 37, how it accepts that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, which counts in the indictment do you say Sikirica is on other than those in which he is named?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Well, on the face of it, paragraph 17 charges him with responsibility for anything which is committed by someone who is a subordinate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, which counts do you understand that to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I've always taken it as being the indictment. The Prosecution's case is he is the commander and therefore the superior authority, and where those acts which are proved as having been committed by subordinates, he is charged with 7(3) responsibility therefor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Strictly speaking, that's a 7(3) responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. It's not individual participation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, perhaps you can help us on this. Is it your case, so that we understand it, that we are to read into -- as Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Mr. Greaves seemed to imply, into virtually every count that you're also charging Sikirica under 7(3) as a superior, or are you, as I had understood it, simply charging those counts in which his name appears?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution is, as Mr. Greaves in fact set forth, that by way of paragraph 17 and paragraph 18, that the accused Sikirica is potentially liable for all of the offences set forth in the indictment on the grounds of Article 7(3) of the statute. In addition, for those articles for which he is specifically listed, for example count 1 and 2, he would in addition be liable under Article 7(1) for those counts in which he is specifically named.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So there are against Sikirica 42 counts, is that right, there being 42 counts in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. In light of the fact, however, that not all of the accused mentioned in the indictment are present in the courtroom, we've certainly focused our, or attempted to focus our evidence on those offences for which the accused are in fact present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So that's 1 to 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: From that, you concede that counts 12 and 13 are not made out?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's correct. The two torture counts, 12 and 13, the Prosecution acknowledges that we have failed to adduce sufficient evidence with respect to those counts. With respect to Mr. Greaves' submissions with respect to the Prosecution acknowledgement concerning Article 7(3) and genocide, that is also correctly stated, of course with no prejudice to the 7(1) case with respect to count 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Since the trial has concentrated on counts 1 to 15, on which these accused are all specifically mentioned, are you inviting us to consider the remaining counts involving other people?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We would invite the Trial Chamber to consider those counts as well, with respect to any count where evidence has in fact been led in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Greaves?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I hope that's now clear. We certainly proceeded on the basis that my learned friend Mr. Mundis has now set out, and so we at least have been proceeding together. Your Honours, as far as other matters are concerned, I would invite you to look at the way in which the Prosecution put their case at the beginning of the trial. I'm not going to read out from the indictment, large chunks of the opening statement made by my learned friend Mr. Ryneveld on the 19th of March, but in my submission, in considering whether or not the Prosecution have in fact satisfied the test that is appropriate for this exercise, it would be right to look at, in the first instance, how it was the Prosecution put the case against Dusko Sikirica at that time. Then the exercise ought to be, we submit, that the reality of what in fact the Prosecution has adduced by way of evidence should be looked at. I address not in any way the issue of quality, save and except in one respect arising out of the Prosecution's reply. Prosecution have demonstrated some evidence that Dusko Sikirica was the commander of Keraterm camp, whatever the phrase "commander" may or may not mean in that context. Although they have adduced that evidence, they have adduced no evidence, we submit, which demonstrates in a positive and direct way what the actual nature of his authority was, what powers were given to him or delegated to him by those who were superior to him; and if he had any sort of power, for example, to punish anybody, they have produced and adduced no evidence whatever to demonstrate what the nature of that power was. Of course, it may be said that there is an inferential state of evidence. For example, if he is in some form of authority, then there may be some inference that he has the power to prevent people from doing things or to punish, but there is no direct evidence as to what the nature of that is. They have produced evidence that during his alleged tenure, there were killings, there were beatings, and there were other -- wide range of other acts by either guards or by persons who had come in from outside Keraterm camp. There is evidence about the conditions of accommodation, of food and water. There is evidence, we accept, that he personally killed people or beat people. And I turn very briefly to deal with one passage in the Prosecution's response concerning that evidence. Prosecution, at paragraph 4 of their reply, say this, at the final sentence: "In the present case, there is conclusive evidence." With the very greatest of respect to the Prosecution, first of all, now is not the time for any such decision to be made as to whether it is conclusive evidence or not. And secondly, we don't for a moment accept in any way that the evidence concerning those incidents is in the least bit conclusive. But it is not appropriate, we submit, that that should be the proposition at this stage. There is evidence there is no -- it should not be a question as to whether it has reached any particular quality or not. There is evidence in the case that in June 1992, he was to be found at a checkpoint at Hambarine. The Prosecution rely on that matter to prove in some way knowledge of events outside the camp. If I can draw Your Honours' attention to page 6 of the Prosecution reply, note 21 in particular. The Prosecution relies in that regard on two pages from the evidence, pages 3710 to 3712. Your Honours, with great respect to the Prosecution, that is a very, very selective piece of noting. There is a substantial portion of evidence from the cross-examination conducted by myself, at pages 3721 to 3727, which forms the evidence in the case, which the Prosecution have simply ignored in making observations about that. If one analyses that evidence, we submit two things in particular: First of all, there is no evidence in relation to that incident that he was present at that checkpoint for anything more than a very short period of time. And again, if you look at that -- the whole of the evidence about that incident, both on examination-in-chief and cross-examination, there is no evidence that around the checkpoint there was anything from which anybody could conclude that there was a genocidal activity taking place. And in particular, the direction in which the witness went and in which things were taking place was away from the checkpoint, and so there is no evidence of any kind that Dusko Sikirica, whilst on the checkpoint at Hambarine that day, saw or was aware of what was going on, and I think the distance that the witness mentions was a substantial one, a kilometre or half a kilometre away. There simply is no evidence, and there simply is no evidence that Sikirica was there for any great length of time, enabling him to look around and see what was going on. And if one looks at what in fact the witness accepts the conversation between him and Sikirica amounted to, we submit that there is nothing in what he finally conceded by way of being the conversation that proves in any way or demonstrates in any way that Sikirica told him to go away because he knew what was going on. There is some evidence that the defendant, on the 5th of August, 1992, read out a list of people who later boarded some buses. However, we respectfully submit that that evidence takes the Prosecution no further forward at all, because if you look at all the evidence concerning that incident, there simply is no evidence at all that the defendant knew where the buses were going, knew what was going to happen to them either at Omarska or after they had left Omarska. The evidence is this, and is only this - and again, I don't address quality at all - the evidence is Dusko Sikirica read out a list of names of people who got on the bus. That is the long and short of that particular evidence. We submit there is no evidence at all of any kind that Dusko Sikirica ever went to Omarska or went to Trnopolje or was in possession of any information of any kind about the events which were taking place at either Omarska or Trnopolje, no evidence of him being in possession of information about conditions which were prevalent at either Omarska or Trnopolje. And it's significant, we respectfully submit, that the only way in which the Prosecution can, apart from evidence about people being transferred to Omarska, the only way in which the Prosecution can connect the defendant, however obliquely, to Omarska, is the incident on the 15th of August, there being evidence, of course, that in fact some of those or all of those who got on the bus did in fact go to Omarska and did in fact -- were almost certainly killed thereafter. That is the only tenuous link that the Prosecution, we say, have adduced as to anything which might amount to a genocidal act in relation to either Omarska or Trnopolje. There is no evidence of any kind whatsoever that the defendant was involved in, knew of, was made party to, given information about, aware of any of the deliberations of, the plans of the Crisis Staff or any other authority, whether it be in Prijedor, Banja Luka, or Republika Srpska, or what is now called Republika Srpska. With the exception of the incident where he is on the checkpoint at Hambarine, there is absolutely nothing in the evidence in this case to show that the defendant knew or was present at or had any information about or ever witnessed or was given anything which would fix him with knowledge of any of the events which took place in the surrounding area around Prijedor or in Prijedor itself, those events which one can give the shorthand phrase "ethnic cleansing" to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But the Prosecution case is that that can be inferred. Knowledge can be inferred, they say, from the widespread nature of the atrocities which were committed, the events in the camp, the conditions in the camp, the killings. And they say, well, you can infer from that that a person in his position knew, must have known, what was the general plan. He may not have been involved in the planning at any high level, they say, but it can be inferred from the events and his position that he must have known what was happening and what the general scheme was, even if he wasn't one of those who planned it. Now, that's the way the case against him is put. Not that he was one of the central planners, as I understand it, or that there's evidence that he was at a meeting at which these things were discussed, because there isn't any evidence, as you've rightly said, but they say you can draw an inference from what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If the only basis, for example, for killings was an obviously genocidal one, that may be possible, but the evidence in the case, in fact, in relation to the motivation for killings is of individuals such as Zoran Zigic using the opportunity to come into the camp, extort money from people; and when those people didn't do as they requested, those people were either ill-treated or in some cases were killed. In relation to the incident in Room 3, there is some suggestion, some evidence, that it may have been because Duca Knezevic had had a relative killed, and that, in any event, it is perfectly plain that that was committed by people who had come in in numbers from outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There is no evidence of genocidal intent and there is evidence to negative -- that tends to negative that intent?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes, in essence. That people like Zoran Zigic and Duca Knezevic were simply acting in a gangster fashion, using the opportunity of having these people there to come in and practise extortion upon them. And it's notable, we say, that in this case -- one can compare it, if I may, with the allegations the Prosecution made in another case in which I was involved, where there were frequent assertions, frequent statements by perpetrators, making reference to balijas and Turks and associating that with what was going to happen to the victims. This case is notable, we submit, by the absence of such language being reported to you in evidence as being associated with the killings, the beatings. We respectfully submit that that is a very significant feature of this case, and if one looks through the transcript, I think there is one -- there are one or two occasions when there are references to people being called Turks or balijas but it is by means -- couldn't be put into the realm of being frequent in this case. And that is extraordinary. If the intention of the Prosecution is that this whole exercise -- and even if he's confined -- if Sikirica is confined to Keraterm, that it can be inferred from this, that there was a genocidal intent behind it, one would expect to find pretty well every witness describing killings as being taking place and accompanied by unpleasant statements such as, "Turk, this is the last dawn you will see," or whatever it is. There are no such things except in one or two very isolated incidents. And that is extraordinary, given the way the Prosecution have put the case and how they describe it, that these killings are not accompanied by such statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not disagreeing with you, Mr. Greaves, but you must remember that the genocidal intent may be inferred not just from killings but also from inflicting on the Bosnian Muslims and Croats particular conditions of life.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Of course, the Prosecution put their case in that way. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not just how -- it's how they put their case; it's also the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: What I meant is they rely on that as one aspect of the genocide. I phrased it badly. But it is significant - and it's a matter that you must take into account, we submit - that there is such a dearth of that kind of evidence. And the killings, however one wants to look at it, they form a central part of the Prosecution's case, and the fact that they are not accompanied by such observations is remarkable, we submit, and indicative that in fact the Prosecution have not indicated and demonstrated that those particular killings were in fact ones which were discriminatory in nature or genocidal in nature. As far as the inferential side of matters is concerned, I would respectfully submit on his behalf that there isn't any evidence that if people were transferred to Omarska or to Trnopolje, that he was aware in any way of what would happen to them or what -- the purpose of sending them either to Omarska or Trnopolje. In relation to the inferential matters that Your Honours raised, we would submit that whilst it is possible so to do, one actually has to look at what in fact -- if the only place in which he can be proved to be and proved to see these events is Keraterm, can one in fact say that there must be a conclusion, or is there a contradictory conclusion which can be drawn from those events? Is the only inference that can be drawn that he must have realised from those facts what was going on in the outside world? Well, the reality is that what was happening is that, with the exception of a small number of women, men of military age are being detained. Beatings and killings are taking place. Those aren't, we submit, demonstrated in a sufficient way to be genocidal killings, and if one looks at the totality of it, we submit that it cannot be said that he was in a position, on the basis of the information available at Keraterm, that it can be said they have demonstrated he could have inferred from those things that there was a genocide taking place. The Prosecution refer to a number of items at paragraph 8 which they draw from their appeals brief in the case of Jelisic. Of course, I hear what Your Honours say about the inferential aspect of it, but it is important and it is a matter that in our submission you should consider, that there is no direct evidence of his knowing of the events outside Keraterm. There is certainly no evidence of him knowing what the general political doctrine was giving rise to these events. There is no evidence that he had positive and direct knowledge of what the scale of the actual or attempted destruction was. There is no evidence that he was aware of any methodical events by way of planning of the killings. And, as far as the systematic manner of killing and disposal of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. bodies is concerned, they rely on the evidence of one particular witness in relation to disposal of bodies. One makes this observation. Firstly, large number -- a number of bodies were buried in the Pasinac cemetery. It is evident from the evidence of that witness that the burials took place in a respectful manner and the bodies were taken there by the town's hearse. With great respect to the Prosecution, those factors are hardly redolent of genocide. It speaks of actually something rather different from that. There is no evidence in the case, we submit, which indicates that out of the mouth of Dusko Sikirica there came discriminatory words or that he had discriminatory thoughts. The absence of those things, we respectfully submit, is remarkable and go very much in this case to an absence of the requisite intent in this case on the part of Dusko Sikirica. I note the time. I have one final observation to make concerning genocide in particular. The cases of Akayesu and Musema make it plain - in the case of Musema at paragraph 175, the judgement, the case of Akayesu, paragraph 532 - that the Prosecution cannot have both complicity in genocide and genocide. What it is said in relation to Akayesu concerning the difference between those two, the Chamber notes, it says, that the logical inference from the foregoing, the paragraphs that come before it, is that an individual cannot thus be both the principal perpetrator of a particular act and the accomplice thereto. An act with which an accused is charged cannot therefore be characterised as both an act of genocide and an act of complicity in genocide. Consequently, since the two are mutually exclusive, the same individual cannot be convicted of both crimes for the same act. And there is a similar reference which I have adverted to in Musema. We respectfully submit that the Prosecution have got to choose. Which is it? Is he guilty of genocide or is he guilty of complicity in genocide? And that the appropriate time for them to choose and elect is now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Greaves, before you finish, can you help us with the point which was raised earlier about the conditions in the camp? There is no dispute, is there, that the conditions were appalling? It relates not only to the genocide, of course, but also other counts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. It would go -- that evidence would go -- I'm loath to adopt Your Honour's phrase "there is no dispute that..." I would say there is evidence in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is evidence and, of course, you've been cross-examining and there has been some evidence of matters which went to mitigate those of those conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes, and you may well hear more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we may well hear more. Is it disputed that the conditions were extremely bad?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I would have to concede that they were not exactly wonderful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And your client was the commander, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: That is the allegation, as it stands today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Greaves. Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I shall endeavour to briefly touch upon what we said in our submission - and we stand by what was said there - and the Prosecutor's response on the 15th of June. First, I should like to refer to counts 12, 13, 14 and 15 of the amended indictment, and these are the counts which have to do with the event -- with the incident, that is the paragraph 45 of the indictment, the period from around the 25th of June, when a group of inmates were called out from Room 2, and that includes Redzep Grabic, and then it said that Damir Dosen, Dusko Knezevic and others severely beat a group of detainees from Room 2, including Grabic. As a result of the beatings, Grabic lost consciousness. As a result of their participation in the above acts, Damir Dosen, Dusko Knezevic committed, count 12, torture, a crime against humanity; count 13, torture, a violation of the laws or customs of war; count 14, inhumane acts, a crime against humanity; count 15, cruel treatment, a violation of the laws or customs of war. And in addition, the indictment says that the accused Damir Dosen is criminally responsible for the crimes set forth in counts 12 to 15 pursuant to Article 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal. And as we say in the -- in our submission, we think that this incident simply never took place because no evidence was adduced before this Tribunal that on or around the 25th of June, did Damir Dosen ever take anybody out from Room 2. Not a single word was said, there is absolutely no evidence that Redzep Grabic, that Redzep Grabic, a person called Redzep Grabic, lost consciousness during that event, that is after he was taken out. We simply believe that the event described in this paragraph or the indictment, paragraph 45, charging our client, and counts 12, 13, 14 and 15, we claim that this event did not happen, that is that so far in the proceedings before this Tribunal, no evidence was adduced to prove that such an incident took place or that the accused Dosen played a part whatever in it -- this. I also wish to point out that the Prosecutor, in their response of the 15th of June this year, submits that - that is the paragraph 3 of the response - that this incident did take place, but in the same paragraph, the Prosecutor admits that Damir Dosen had no part in this event or, rather, admitted that the nature of his participation in this event, that the role attributable to Damir Dosen, the only kind -- the nature of Damir Dosen's during that incident is exculpatory. I also point out that in the last of the -- in the last sentence of paragraph 3 of Prosecutor's response, the Prosecution acknowledges that the accused Dosen should be acquitted with respect to liability for counts 12, 13, 14, and 15 of the amended indictment. That also subsumes that he should be acquitted of the charge pursuant to Article 7(3), that is, his responsibility for what happened there, and I therefore expect from the Trial Chamber to acquit Damir Dosen of liability for these counts, for these four counts in the indictment, for reasons that I have just quoted. As regards paragraph 17 of our submission of the 8th of June, the Defence, having analysed the evidence produced before this Tribunal and listed therefor 23 names and then another list of 6 names of people who are in confidential annex to the indictment and who are represented as people who were victims of the incidents in Keraterm and who the Defence affirms were in no way associated with the evidence that has been adduced so far before this Chamber. Before I address some of these names, I should like to indicate first the defence of Mr. Dosen's defence [as interpreted] that when it comes to this aspect of our submission, there is perhaps room for this Trial Chamber to -- in deciding on the responsibility of the accused under different counts of the indictment, the Trial Chamber may also take a view and assess various documents in annexes to the indictment. And this is based on the decisions of other Trial Chambers of this Tribunal which we quote in our submission, and there is no need to go back to them. In its response, the Prosecutor accepts that the names of six people indicated in annex A relative to Damir Dosen were not mentioned in any way in any exhibit, in any piece of evidence adduced so far, and this is paragraph 4 of the Prosecutor's response. Furthermore, I should like to point out that a name -- and I should like to read those names out, so I hope this will be granted. These are the names of Jasmin Cepic, Suvad Cehic, Velid Dizdarevic, Fajzo Halilovic, Fahrudin Hrustic, and Refik Oruc. One of the names, in our submission, is the name of a person who is in the annex to the indictment, which is an integral part of the indictment, is also the name of a man called Agan Duratovic. There is, we submit, not a single piece of evidence that that person was involved in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. any way whatsoever in whatever happened in Keraterm. The Prosecutor does not address this person, I do not know whether by omission or whatever reason, but they neither challenge nor confirm our submission that that person was in any way whatsoever involved in the matter under discussion. However, there is another fact that I wish to mention, and that is that the name -- there are names of eight persons on this list, and it is submitted that there is evidence in this case in relation to them and that they should remain on the list in confidential annex A. It is a group of persons who were exhumed and identified at a place called Hrastova Glavica. These are eight names, and the evidence adduced before this Tribunal, they were never mentioned, either in the testimonies of witnesses who testified here or in other evidence produced before this Chamber. They are not mentioned in any of those instances. They are mentioned only in one document which allegedly relates these people to the Keraterm camp. That is, these are persons for whom no evidence has produced that they were ever in Keraterm, that they had anything to do with Keraterm, and these are persons about which the only certain knowledge we have is that they were exhumed at Hrastova Glavica, that they were identified subsequent to that, but no relationship has been established between the exhumation, the death of these people, and the things that happened in Keraterm. These are persons whose names I will now read out, and they are Hasan Basic, Ferid Brkic, Refik Damirovic, Sefik Ferhatovic, Raif Hopovac, Mujo Pasic, Senad Resic, and Mustafa Svraka. The Prosecutor, in their response, refer to the expert report and say that they are persons who were exhumed at the location at Hrastova Glavica. But the only relationship between these eight persons who are in the confidential annex to the indictment and the Keraterm camp is a document, or rather, the record of the cantonal court in Bihac on the exhumation of these persons on the 5th of December, 1998, and the only link between the exhumed persons and -- that is the only link between these persons and the -- and the Keraterm is one sentence on page 2 of the Bosnian version of this document, which says that on the basis of information collected and the exhumation of the persons, it was established at some time in the summer of 1992 from the Serb camp of Keraterm a certain number of persons were taken in two buses from the direction of the municipality of Sanski Most, and it is assumed that these persons were taken there to the place of execution, and so on and so forth. So this sentence says that through the information collected and statements of survivors, this Trial Chamber did not hear what information was collected, what testimony, statements of survivors are concerned. We heard a number of witnesses, and yet in relation to the persons that I mentioned a while ago, there is not -- not a single link has been shown here to exist between these people and their unfortunate death and Keraterm camp. So this is all -- doesn't go beyond assumption, and we think that in relation to these eight persons whose names we have mentioned, that the Trial Chamber should decide that the names of these people should be stricken out from the confidential list insofar as my client, Damir Dosen, is concerned. I hope that I clarified our -- that I made our position clear to the Trial Chamber. And if you believe -- if the Trial Chamber considers it relevant, the Trial Chamber may seek further explanation, and I shall try to provide it. It all concerns the confidential annex A to this indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, just let me clarify what you are saying. The eight names that you read out, are they not among the list in paragraph 5 on page 4 of the Prosecution's response as persons who were detained in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. These are persons who, according to the Prosecutor's response, are from letters E to P of the list which is on page 5 of the Prosecutor's response and footnotes from 17 to 24. They show that these are persons who were exhumed at Hrastova Glavica. What I am trying to say is that no other link has been shown between these persons from Hrastova Glavica and Keraterm except the report on the exhumation of the cantonal court in Bihac. No other link between the two has ever been shown except a general claim where -- a general claim in this report of the cantonal court in Bihac, which is according to the information collected and testimonies of the survivors. Nothing else. And this sentence doesn't seem to suffice in itself. This sentence is part of the record of the cantonal court, or rather, the investigative magistrate of the cantonal court in Bihac, and he's the only one that establishes a link on the basis of some information that he is privy to. But apart from his claim to that effect, there is nothing else about it, and that is why we believe that, in addition to the six names - and the Prosecution admits that they have absolutely no evidence - there are also these -- there is also the person Duratovic. The Prosecution never mentioned them. In addition to them, we also think that these eight names should also be stricken out from the list in the confidential annex A to the indictment because not a minimal shred of evidence has been shown here, has been produced here, to show a link between these persons and Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that clarification, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I should further like to say a few words about what is implied in the indictment against my client, and that is the link between his behaviour and the camps in Omarska and Trnopolje. The Defence does not believe that this discussion, pursuant to Article 28, is not an occasion for discussing whether certain acts were committed in Omarska, Trnopolje, and Keraterm, and whether they represent part of a general pattern of persecution of non-Serb population in this area. It is our opinion that the very fact that certain crimes may have been committed is not sufficient for the commission of those crimes to be linked to the accused. We need to speak about the specific role of the accused, in this case the accused Damir Dosen, and his part in those events, and there is no link to show that Damir Dosen is in any way linked to the events which occurred in Omarska and Trnopolje. There is no evidence adduced to support that. The only link that the Prosecutor is trying to establish is the allegation that on the 5th of August, 1992, he was present when lists of names were read out of people who were apparently sent to Omarska. This can be seen from a statement of one witness, but that statement does not show that Damir Dosen had any kind of knowledge as to where those people were going or what would happen to them subsequently. The only thing that witness states in his statement is that he was present, and I underline that this is only one witness who made that testimony. No other link between those events and Dosen were adduced, and we feel that that is no basis for finding that Damir Dosen, as implied in paragraph 7, 8, 9, and 10 of the indictment, is linked to the events that occurred in Omarska and Trnopolje. And of course, I don't think there is any need for me to repeat what my learned friend Mr. Greaves has already said, because much of what he said can also apply to my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You reject, then, the Prosecution's case of a common criminal purpose, of common design, an integral part of which, according to the Prosecution, were the three camps?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. As far as I'm able to understand, and we have all been listening and seeing, there is simply no evidence to prove that allegation. Very briefly, let me say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The point of the common design is that the various actions take place not necessarily involving the particular accused, but what is alleged is that he played his part in the common design, albeit at Keraterm, but that there was a much larger design involving the other camps too - this is the Prosecution case - and that although there's no evidence that your client was at Omarska or Trnopolje, nonetheless, the fact that he was playing his part - this is what the Prosecution say -- at Keraterm, means that he was part of the common design involving all three camps. Do you say there's no evidence sufficient to support a common design involving all three camps and involving the Bosnian Muslim population in Prijedor, common design to keep them in the camps in those sort of conditions, to kill some, to subject them to beatings? Do you say there's no evidence on which we can find there was such a common design?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would not call it a common design. I would talk about the awareness and knowledge of my client as to him being a part of any such common design. I am not taking a position as to any such thing existed in the territory of Prijedor municipality and who is responsible for that. I'm just saying that Damir Dosen, the position he held and the knowledge and abilities he commanded simply had no awareness that any such design existed, which I allow may have existed, nor that he was in any way a part of it. So when I refer to it, I'm talking about his awareness of being a part of any such common design. He had no such awareness. He had no idea of being a part of any such plan or common design. That is what we are submitting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. With regard to the last part of our submission, I should just like to make a few points, and those are that there is only a very generalised allegation that Damir Dosen, sometimes he is called shift commander or shift leader, and this allegation has been void of any real content. It is true that a certain number of Prosecution witnesses did say that that man was a shift leader or a shift komandir, but it is also true that this Trial Chamber has not seen any evidence as to the substance of this position of shift leader. No evidence has been adduced to indicate what kind of authority such a person had, from where that authority is derived and how it could be exercised. No indication whatsoever has been given as to the substance of those powers. Also, there is a significant amount of evidence to show that Damir Dosen did not in any way participate in the establishment of what is called Keraterm. He did not participate in deciding where the people would be accommodated or in distributing the people into those premises, that he had no influence over the food supply or the water or the electricity supply. All the witnesses that we have heard said that the food was brought in from outside, from a location they are unaware of. They all also said that the water was brought in from another location which they are unaware of. Nobody said that the frequency of the arrival of that water depended on Damir Dosen in any way, nor that he had any role in deciding whether people would lie on wooden pallets or on concrete floors. Damir Dosen -- and again there was no evidence to show that, that Damir Dosen had any influence over the transfer of people to Omarska or anywhere else. The only thing that we heard was that he was the shift commander or komandir, but nothing to indicate the substance of that role, that he had any kind of authority over the people who were, according to the statements of some witnesses, working in his shift, what means he had at his disposal, legal or otherwise, to punish them, what competencies he had and where they were derived from. This was a mobilised man, without a single day of training, who found himself in this position, and even if he had any kind of authority, had no training or power to implement that authority. Simply, the Prosecution case in that segment is based on suppositions that, being the shift commander, he had a certain authority, but no evidence was adduced to show what kind of authority he had over what was happening in Keraterm, not counting what any normal person would try to do, as far as he is able, when he sees somebody in trouble. So as a human being, he wants to assist him, but not on the basis of any kind of authority, about which, I wish to underline once again, no concrete evidence was presented to Your Honours. I have nothing more to add. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Sir Ivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: May it please the Chamber. In our respectful submission, firstly, our submission on the written motion for judgement of acquittal fairly explains why there is no prima facie case for the Defence to answer, on any of the five counts, whether under Article 1 or -- Article 7(1) or Article 7(3). And secondly, we submit that the Prosecution's response does not adequately answer those submissions. May I begin with the question of the standard under review? We submit that the test is as set out in the most recent Rule 98 bis judgement in the Kunarac case. That is, whether there is evidence upon which a reasonable Tribunal of fact - yourselves - could be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt of the guilt of the accused on the particular charge in question. That was specifically related to Rule 98 bis. The Prosecution say that the test is clearly not one of reasonable doubt at this stage. They say that the Rule 98 bis is not a proper procedural setting to discuss the law and that, for the purpose of Rule 98 bis, all reasonable inferences should be drawn in favour of the Prosecution. For all of these propositions, they cite as authority themselves in their application in the Jelisic appeal, and they cite themselves because there appears to be no other authority for those propositions since they appear to demonstrate, in our respectful submission, a lack of understanding of the procedures of criminal trial in all states which recognise the ordinary concepts of the rule of law. Firstly, in all such states, the burden of proof is always on the Prosecution, and where there is conflict, inferences should, where possible, be drawn in favour of the Defence, not in favour of the Prosecution. We could cite the authority of United Kingdom law, of United States law, and the law of the British Commonwealth. Secondly, this 98 bis procedure is the proper procedural setting to discuss fully the law applicable to the charges. Again, this is clearly the position at the end of the Prosecution case in the United Kingdom, in the United States, and were it different, there would be something in Rule 98 bis to that effect. But there is nothing in either (A) or (B) which seeks to change the common law position. Thirdly, it's true that the words cited in the Prosecution response from the Kordic and Cerkez case, which was earlier than the Kunarac case, says that the true test is not one of reasonable doubt, but with respect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is just a matter I want to discuss.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Sir Ivan, help us with this: What's the difference between -- as you see it, between what this Chamber said in Kordic and what another Chamber said in Kunarac? Is there a difference?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I'm dealing with it. May I take you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: If I don't deal with it, perhaps Your Honour would be good enough to tell me. It's true that the words cited in Kordic - if I can call it the Kordic case, which I've suggested is earlier than the Kunarac case - says that the true test is not one of reasonable doubt, but with respect, that judgement is ambiguous since it goes on to say that the test is whether there is evidence on which a reasonable Tribunal - I'm sorry, a reasonable Chamber - could convict, and since a reasonable Chamber could only convict if it was satisfied beyond reasonable doubt --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please read more slowly?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: [No microphone] ... not be taken as prevailing over Kunarac which is clearer, unambiguous and later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But the important point is, the important distinction I think we were making in Kordic is that, at this stage, the Trial Chamber does not have to ask itself, "Are we satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that the accused -- if the case ended here, we would convict the accused on this evidence?" I think this is the distinction. We are not -- I'm sorry, let me finish. We are not asking ourselves, "Suppose the case finishes now; do we convict?" We are asking ourselves, "Could we, were the case to finish now, convict?" And I think the distinction is this: We are not applying the proof-beyond-reasonable-doubt test, which is of course what is applied at the end of the case, at this stage. We are applying the test: Is there evidence on which we could be satisfied were we to ask ourselves that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: My response to that, Your Honour, is that that is a distinction without a difference. It's an artificial distinction, because any Tribunal throughout the western world placed in the position -- in this particular stage, and in a jurisdiction where decisions of fact are not to be taken by a jury but where the Tribunal is itself the court of fact, has to decide at the earliest moment - and the bis 98 situation is the earliest moment - whether it wants to go on, whether it should go on. So not just, "Could we" but "Must we" is really the test that ought to apply, and for reasons -- can I explain why I say that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me put this point to you; test it this way: Suppose you are right about that and we are asking ourselves, "Would we now convict?" That could mean this: If you chose to call no evidence, if the Defence chose to call no evidence, and simply said, "That's it, we are not calling any evidence," it would be a pointless exercise because we would have already made our minds up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Certainly so, but that applies in our jurisdiction back in the United Kingdom. The Defence must never be put -- and this is even clearer now that we are signed up to the United Nations -- the European Convention of Human Rights, the Defence must never be put in a position where the burden transfers to them unless they have a case to answer because there is a prima facie case; the Tribunal at the midway stage, at the end of the Prosecution case, is satisfied that there is a case to answer. If they were to make the judgement then, they would say -- they would say there is reasonable doubt, and that provided that the Chamber is one which is the tribunal of fact. All that happens, if you let the matter go further, is the Defence have another bite at the cherry. What can then happen is that if the court says, "We are satisfied beyond reasonable doubt at this stage. If you want to, you can call evidence and place a doubt in our mind, because you call evidence that conflicts with the evidence that's already been given by the Prosecution," but there is still a stage earlier at which the court must decide whether the Prosecution case is so conflicting, so full of holes, so unsubstantial, insufficient, inadequate, that the only proper course is to say, "We are not satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt at this stage." Can I - it may be clearer - just develop my reasons a little bit further? I would suggest, with great respect, that we go back to Rule 98 bis itself, which states at section (B) - which is presumably envisaging the same test as applies in section (A), although it doesn't say so - the judgement of acquittal shall be entered if the Tribunal finds that the evidence is insufficient to sustain a conviction. Sustaining a conviction means beyond reasonable doubt. It says nothing about whether some evidence is enough, however unsatisfactory, which seems to be the Prosecution's submission. And in our respectful submission, in deciding whether the evidence is insufficient to sustain a conviction, the Chamber has to consider firstly whether there is any evidence at all of the vital element in the offence. If not, an acquittal must follow. And secondly, if there is some evidence, the Chamber must consider whether it's sufficient. That's what it says in the rule. That can only mean sufficient as to quantity or sufficient as to quality to prove beyond reasonable doubt the guilt of the accused, on the assumption that has to be made --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sir Ivan, there has been a request for you to slow down for the interests of the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: On the assumption that there is no more evidence forthcoming. And if there is no sufficient evidence, then an acquittal must follow. And may I make these observations in support of this submission, and it's more closely in answer to what Your Honour has just asked me: Although the Kordic case did rule that generally the Chamber wouldn't consider questions of credibility and reliability in dealing with a motion under Rule 98 bis, it did go on to say that there is one situation in which the Chamber is obliged to consider such matters, and that's where the Prosecution case has completely broken down as a result of such fundamental questions raised through cross-examination as to the reliability and credibility of witnesses so that the Prosecution is left without a case. And we say that that's what's happened here, that fundamental questions have been raised about the reliability of witnesses, as well as the very existence of any evidence on some of the accusations made against Kole. And secondly, if the Chamber was not allowed to consider the reliability of witnesses, as well as the existence of any evidence at this stage, the situation would be that a tribunal whose members knew that they were not going to convict because they could never be satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt on the evidence they have heard, would have to sit there for months at great expense in money and resources to the United Nations, and time, as well as trauma to witnesses and the defendant, and the situation would be absurd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. As I understand it, the Rule 98 bis more or less follows the common law position, and that position, based on a reading of the law in the United Kingdom, the United States, other Commonwealth countries, is not that at the halfway stage there must be evidence which satisfies the Tribunal beyond a reasonable doubt, but that the evidence must raise a possibility of conviction, not that the evidence must establish the certainty of conviction. In both cases, proof beyond a reasonable doubt is involved, but the prima facie test merely calls for the possibility, as a matter of law, of proof beyond reasonable doubt, not the certainty. Now, the Kordic case, in which Judge May and I were involved, went a little further and reflected the general position in the common law, which is that at the halfway stage, as a general rule, as a matter of principle, the Tribunal is not concerned with issues of credibility and reliability except where, as you have pointed out, the case has completely broken down because of fundamental discrepancies in the Prosecution evidence. I understand that you are saying that your case falls within that. You're saying that the Prosecution case in respect of your client is so riddled with inconsistencies and discrepancies that your client should not be called on to answer. But I principally wanted to explain that, on the basis of the Kordic case, if we ruled that there was a case to answer, we would not be involved in a futile exercise, as you say, and a waste of the United Nations' funds because we are really saying nothing more than that the evidence raises a possibility, as a matter of law, of proof beyond reasonable doubt, not a certainty. When we come to the final stage, we look at that evidence which at the halfway stage we said raises the possibility of conviction, and ask ourselves whether we are now certain beyond reasonable doubt of the guilt of the accused persons. That is how -- that's my understanding of the general position in the common law, which I believe Rule 98 bis seeks to reflect.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I agree with Your Honour. The point I make is that the question about whether there is a possibility, and the question about whether the defendant ought to be acquitted or not, is a distinction without a difference. That is to say, that if you came to the conclusion that there was a possibility, if no more was said, that he would be convicted in the end, but only a possibility, which means that there wouldn't be a reasonable -- a decision beyond reasonable doubt that he ought to be convicted, and no evidence is called, and no evidence happens which might add to it, at the end of the day, the court is in a position of saying, "Well, it's possible he's guilty but we can't say he's guilty beyond a reasonable doubt." So you would have sat there for months at great expense and at great waste of time. It's a common sense position really, and the law hopefully from time to time follows common sense. If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, Sir Ivan, but you are not right on this particular point. There is a distinction, because what you're asking us to do is to ask ourselves this: "Are we satisfied beyond reasonable doubt of the guilt of your accused on this evidence?" Suppose we say, "Yes, we are satisfied beyond reasonable doubt, upon the evidence, of your client's guilt," we then throw a burden upon your client, which we are not entitled to do, to show why he's not guilty. The distinction is the possibility, as a matter of law, that we could make that finding, not that we are making it. And that is a very important distinction. And it would be quite wrong for the law to proceed on the basis that at this stage, the halfway stage in the trial, chambers are deciding on the guilt or otherwise of accused beyond reasonable doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: You can't say a man is guilty at this stage because you haven't heard all he might want to say, but you can say that a man is innocent at this stage, and that's what the processes do. That's why Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. submissions of no case to answer frequently succeed in the United Kingdom, the United States and other Commonwealth countries, because although the court isn't saying, "We are satisfied of guilt" - the court mustn't say that; the court isn't allowed to say that - the court is merely saying that, "It's possible at the end of the day we may be sure." What they are saying is that the Prosecution certainly have not produced sufficient, adequate evidence to reach first base.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: It may be that it's unnecessary for me to be arguing this, and it may be that if Your Lordships are right -- Your Honours are right, it still doesn't make any difference to my argument because what I've indicated is that the Defence case comes four-square under Kordic and Kunarac anyway, because we say that the insufficiency is so fundamental. So may I proceed along that line?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The only point I raise is whether the test needs clarification or not. If it's not clear between Kordic and Kunarac which is the test to be applied, then it may be that we should clarify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: In my respectful submission, the Tribunal ought to, if for no other reason than the one I've already given, and that is that there is an ambiguity in Kordic which says that the reasonable doubt test doesn't apply but goes on to say that the test is whether there is evidence upon which a reasonable tribunal could convict, and provided the court is with me on a distinction between the way in which it must look at the matter from the Defence point of view or from the Prosecution point of view, then there is an ambiguity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't think so. What that means simply is that the test is not the certainty of conviction of proof beyond reasonable doubt but the possibility of conviction on the basis of proof beyond reasonable doubt, and that's what Kordic clarified in the subsequent sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: The point I make in answer to Your Honours is that the possibility is a matter which the Defence may want to address in order to dispel, but if the Defence don't do that, do not choose to do that, then the court is left in the position where all they are saying is that there is a possibility but we can't be certain beyond a reasonable doubt at the end. So they will have sat there for nothing if the Defence don't grasp the nettle and run with it. Or they will not have sat there for nothing, of course, if the court is satisfied that there is a sufficiency of evidence to put them in that situation. Anyway, the court has said quite clearly that if there are fundamental questions about reliability of witnesses, et cetera, then you will consider that, and that is what sufficiency of evidence must mean: quality and quantity to some extent in some circumstances. And it's particularly relevant, but in my respectful submission not exclusively so, because we have here an identification issue, and Kunarac's gloss is that consideration of reliability of identification evidence is of particular concern, and Kunarac considered what we call in the United Kingdom the Turnbull provisions which may lead a Chamber to conclude that if the evidence of identification is not capable of being established beyond reasonable doubt that the accused is the offender, because it's unreliable in that sense, then even if the evidence to which the Prosecution have pointed is accepted, that evidence is insufficient to sustain a conviction. And the authorities keep saying, insufficient to sustain a conviction. They say that at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Sir Ivan, we are well past 11.00. You will be allowed to continue after.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I'm most grateful, and I'm sorry but it does seem to me, in my respectful submission, to be an important basis of the Prosecution's response to Kolundzija's Defence that they don't have to do any more than adduce some evidence, and that later on, at the end of the trial, in three months' time, the Tribunal will be -- the Chamber will be considering whether there is a reasonable doubt at the end. And in my respectful submission, I have to deal with that, and I hope that I've done with it. Can I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sir Ivan, we are going to take the break now and when we resume, you will be allowed to continue. May I just say that in common law jurisdictions, it has happened that a tribunal of fact has ruled case to answer, Defence rests, calls no evidence, and at the end of the day, the man is acquitted, and that illustrates the classical distinction between the burden at the halfway stage and what happens at the final stage. And that is the result of nothing more than that the burden ultimately is on the Prosecution to establish proof beyond a reasonable doubt. And I don't call that a waste of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I agree with that, but the fact remains, looking at it in realistic terms, if all the Tribunal is doing is saying, "Well, there is a possibility, but if we were called to decide the matter now, we would throw the case out," then the effect, realistic effect is that you will sit there for three months, the Defence will sit on their hands, and you will be driven to the conclusion you would have come to if you'd given yourselves the opportunity to do it. So that the evidence at this bis 98 stage is simply insufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let us continue at 20 minutes to 12.00. We are adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Sir Ivan. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: May it please the Chamber. One last point --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: One last point on the law. If it is right, as the Chamber is suggesting, that could secure a conviction is the right test, may I be permitted to ask: Why does Rule 98 bis not say so? Why doesn't it say evidence which could result in a conviction, and why does it say, to the contrary, that an acquittal shall follow --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sir Ivan, would you please stop. There is no interpretation in French. Would that be looked into, please. Is there a technical problem? We now have the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Why does it not say so? Why does it say, to the contrary, that acquittal shall follow at this stage if the evidence is not sufficient to sustain a conviction?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Sir Ivan, the answer to that is, in my view, quite simple. The Statute is to be interpreted like a treaty, and quite often you find language in a treaty which does not have the literal meaning that one would normally ascribe to it. To derive the proper interpretation, you have to do a variety of things, including, most importantly, interpreting the provision in the context in which it is written; and the context here is predominantly the common law at jurisdiction and regime. So we still -- we have to determine what is meant by "insufficient" here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: And what we are asking the Court to decide at this stage is that the evidence, as far as Kole is concerned, on all of those five counts and their Article 7(3) alternatives, is sufficient. We suggest it is not sufficient and we suggest that under the heading of fundamental insufficiency, we're entitled, under the Kordic/Kunarac principles, to have that challenged here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are not against you, I think, on that. If we found that the evidence was insufficient or could not sustain a conviction, if it had broken down, whatever phrase you choose to use, clearly it's the Trial Chamber's duty to stop the case and not go on in what you describe as a futile exercise of sitting there, knowing it's never going to be sufficient. What I'm anxious to avoid is any notion that the Trial Chamber should apply the test, the eventual test in deciding on conviction, on whether to convict somebody at this particular stage. But I think it's a semantic difference, and we're not going to get any further by debating it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Not to convict, but to acquit, and I make the distinction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As far as your submission is concerned, I'm sure we're with you to this extent: that it's open to us at this stage, if we don't think the evidence is sufficient to sustain a conviction, not only is it open to us; we must acquit. But if it could sustain a conviction, that's another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Clearly, the question of mistaken identity arises in the case against Kolundzija as far as the evidence of Witness N is concerned. We say that it's fundamental, it affects both the reliability of the witness and whether there is any evidence at all against Kolundzija on this point. And yet, we submit, the Prosecution have totally failed to address either the evidence or even the procedural situation which arises in their response. They've just not dealt with it. They have hidden behind the "not now; later" theory. And so I submit that the Prosecutor's response under Roman I to our submissions should be rejected. So going to Witness N, who forms one of the substantial planks in counts 3, 4 and 5 against Kolundzija, on what we can broadly call the mistreatment counts, and which the Prosecution refer to eight times, both in the main text and footnotes in their response, as though the witness is reliable; and the reliability is in dispute, and I've set out the ten reasons why we submit that the evidence of identification of Kolundzija as a beater and permitter of beatings is fatally flawed -- is so fatally flawed that it falls four-square under the Kordic-Kunarac principle. And that's in our written submission at page 5, paragraph 3, a to k. The court will remember how the case was opened in this matter by my learned friend for the Prosecution, at page 507, lines 4 to 16: "Although most witnesses say that fewer beatings took place on Kolundzija's shift, the overall conditions in the camp on his shift were as terrible as during the other shifts. Several witnesses recall at least four occasions when Kole was present during beatings. More specifically, witnesses will tell you that Kolundzija was present and participated when prisoners were beaten with iron bar, rifles, bats, planks and batons. One recalls an incident where Kole ordered a prisoner to go outside; shortly afterwards, two shots were heard. Even more particularly, one witness will tell you that Kolundzija beat him with a stick. He claims that, along with two other prisoners, he was beaten by Kolundzija until he lost consciousness. And we expect you will hear from witnesses that Kolundzija was also present when the Banovic brothers and a guard named Grujin would beat the prisoners while they were eating." And most of that, if not all of it, refers to Witness N. Well, what was the evidence? The evidence is set out at page 6, as I have indicated, and I needn't repeat because of the shortage of time. How does the Prosecution respond to this? Page 6, paragraph 9: "Paragraph 3 on Page 5 of the Kolundzija Rule 98 bis Submission relates entirely to issues of argument concerning the issue of reliability of evidence relating to identification of Kolundzija." This is a matter which has got to be delayed as to weight. "There is, at present, some evidence upon which, if accepted, the Trial Chamber could reasonably convict. The various witnesses ascribed the conduct to Kolundzija. These witnesses learned his identity from others in the camp who knew Kolundzija before he was employed at Keraterm." But those witnesses, who weren't produced but we heard about them from Witness N, weren't present at any of the three incidents which Witness N describes. So how can they identify Kolundzija? It's not just hearsay, it's double hearsay of identification, which under any common law jurisdiction cannot be valid. We submit that that response is not an answer, and that the evidence on that major matter of identification is fatally flawed. Another plank in the Prosecution's case on mistreatment is the evidence of O, which was adduced to show that Kolundzija was present at a beating and did nothing about it. She told us that she was there at the gate, if you recall, when the bus from Brdo arrived. Obviously, mere presence is not enough, as evidence of an intention or as evidence of a participation, to establish guilt. We deal with her evidence at page 7 of the written submission, at paragraph 4, and submit that her evidence fell short of such proof because she said that at the moment the beating started, she left.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: (redacted) and I can make various assumptions that he went and stopped them but I have no knowledge of that. Immediately when you saw this happen, Dragan Kolundzija told you you should go? Yes. At that moment, he told you to go? Yes. In my respectful submission, it's clear that that passage is no evidence against Kolundzija, and it's so fundamental a matter as to fall four-square into the Kordic-Kunarac principle. Prosecution refer to other evidence of Kolundzija being present at beatings. And look how, at paragraph 10, at page 6, they deal with that. And in my respectful submission, their examples are wholly selective and unfair. They were forced to lie in the hot sun, called out to be beaten and were denied food and water. This is leading up to it. Well, the first authority, B, said that Kole allowed food to Room 3, there was no beating occurring during Kole's shift, and there was no suggestion that he was responsible for any of the situations under consideration. C said Kole was the best, there was no beating on his shift, and there was no suggestion that Kole was responsible for the mistreatment of Brdo inmates. F, no suggestion that Kole was responsible. He said that Kole wasn't present when any beating took place. Arifagic only thought it was Kole who was on duty when Banovic and Kondic called people out. H was not sure whether Aliskovic was taken out on Fustar, Kole, or Kajin's shift. M said the calling out was done before Kole's shift and that he never had had better -- felt treatment than under Kole. N I've dealt with. That's the identification witness. That's wheeled out. And so on. I won't go through all of it, in the interests of time. Because this treatment lasted over a period of some days, my learned friend says, given the shift structure, it can be inferred that it continued during Kole's shift as well. Well, can it? They came on the 20th of July. Kole was only on two shifts, if the shift roster spoken about by several witnesses is taken as a guide. That was on the 21st of July, at night, and the 23rd of July in the day, before the massacre took place. So there wasn't a great deal of opportunity, and the witnesses are very unspecific. One witness indicated that they were locked up regardless of whose shift was on, but the evidence is they were locked up for their own safety. B: In fact, a witness indicated during this period of detention Kole and his group arrived and started beating the prisoners, although Kole himself did not personally beat them. That's N relied upon again. C: One witness said that they were beaten on all shifts, but less so on Kole's shift. That was Arifagic, who, as I pointed out, only thought Kole was on duty when Banovic and Kordic were there. And another said that prisoners were called out on Kole's shift but less often. That, in my respectful submission, is much too vague a statement to convict anybody, if taken alone. D: One witness indicated that Kole was present when the Muslims hodza was beaten, but that witness misidentified Dosen as Kolundzija. It doesn't strengthen the reliability of that witness to say he later indicated he had been mistaken about the identification. E: According to old Witness 9 again, wheeled out. F: Witness O. That's the lady at the gate again, wheeled out. Witness X and G also indicated that Kolundzija was present at a number of beatings. In my respectful submission, that's very unfair, and you were referred to pages 4020, 4026 and 4127, but you weren't referred to paragraphs 412 - sorry - page 4129, at line 21, to page 4130, at paragraph 20. Can I just read you what that said?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the one occasion that you could remember an incident where he was present in August of 2000, he was trying to stop the beating, you've told us; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. So there he is present at a beating but trying to stop it. At line 4 at page 4130:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On this second occasion, was Kole trying to stop that beating as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not see that. I could not hear it, because it was so far. I could see, but how can I know what he tried and if he tried anything?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your answer is that you don't know whether he was trying to stop it or not; you really don't know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you never saw Kole taking part in any mistreatment of any prisoner; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was never an active participant in the mistreatment or killing of any Keraterm detainee; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see it. Maybe somebody else did. I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you could see, he was never an active participant in the mistreatment or killing of any Keraterm detainee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see it. Is it, in those circumstances, fair for the Prosecution to say, at subparagraph G, Witness X also indicated that Kolundzija was present at a number of beatings, with the implication that he did nothing except approve them? H is just as bad. According to Witness M, at dusk on the day of massacre, 20 prisoners were beaten, 15 of them from Room 3, and page 2705 was referred to. But what wasn't referred to was page 2803, at line 6, to page 2804, at line 11, and page 2823, lines 1 to 8. Can I read, at any rate, the first of those?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The calling out of the 20 prisoners from the rooms by Faca. Is that how you pronounce his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That happened in the afternoon of the day of the massacre, did it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somewhere around there, towards dusk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that in your interview you said on the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. There was only one incident like that that happened that afternoon, was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Put a time on it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Towards dusk, perhaps around 6.00 to 7.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Might it have been earlier than 6.00?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps before 6.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your recollection is that the shift changed at about 7.00 at that time, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall exactly. There were changes. Then over the page:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know you can't be definite and specific about times, but your impression is - it's the impression that matters - your impression is that the shift changed at around 7.00 in the evening, at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that the calling-out incident took place at about 6.00, but it may have been earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that I think the impression you're intending to convey is that the calling-out incident took place before the end of the shift.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was Fustar's shift, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't recall exactly whose shift it was, but they were all there. They were all all mixed in together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it was -- can you recall that Kole's shift was in the evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kole's shift was in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your recollection is that the calling out took place before Kole's shift. Whoever's shift it was, it was before Kole's shift?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was all around that time, during that transition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
