utterances.text: You told me just now that your impression is the shift changed around 7.00. You've told me just now that your impression was that the calling out took place at about 6.00 or maybe earlier. All right? Nothing wrong so far?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And therefore the calling out must have taken place before the evening shift?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if the evening shift was Kole's shift, which everyone says it was, then the calling out didn't take place during Kole's shift; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct. And I won't read the other reference, but it's, as far as I can recall, to the same effect. So H is unfair, and you haven't been given all of the relevant references that correct 2705 that you were given. I: Not only were the Brdo area prisoners in room 3 inhumanely treated, but all the detainees were subject to inhumane treatment during their detention, were the subject of persecution, to which my comment is: Yes, but that statement doesn't prove that Kolundzija either, A, participated; still less does it prove that he was willing in the participation. In my respectful submission, the Prosecution's response to our written submission is neither adequate nor is it an answer. The basis of the Prosecution's case on counts 3, 4, and 5 is then set out at page 4, paragraph 5 of the response. It describes what persecution is, outrages, violation of the laws and customs of war, common-purpose liability - Kolundzija was one of hundreds - to which my observation is: Yes, but there must be some evidence that "Kole" Kolundzija, was a willing party to this, and there must be some evidence that Kolundzija knew that ethnic cleansing was going on in other parts of the country, and there must be some evidence that he knew about Omarska and Trnopolje; some evidence, but there's none. And if anybody says, "Ah, well, everybody must have known," you heard Mr. Vulliamy giving evidence, saying that at the time all this was happening, he unfortunately drove right past Keraterm on his way to Omarska, had no idea what was going on there. So as to common-purpose liability, I don't take issue with the principle. What I take issue with is whether there's any evidence that Kole was knowingly, willingly involved. Then the issue of shift commander is raised. Our argument has already been referred to by my learned friends on this matter, and at paragraph 6 the Prosecution deal with it. They assert that the Prosecution has failed to prove that the accused had sufficient authority as the shift commander to exercise control over other guards on his shift in order to make life more bearable, is the text. An inference can be drawn that he had the requisite authority. How? I ask. Why? There's a need to prove that the authority which he undoubtedly had, to a limited extent -- there's no dispute that guards asked him questions, that he was the shift leader, but the question is whether his authority spread beyond that, as is set out in the Pre-Trial brief, authority to discipline and punish. Now, that can't be inferred, particularly if, as the Prosecution say, there's no evidence that he did discipline or punish anyone. What the Prosecution surely have to do is to produce a document or a live witness to say that the office of shift commander has with it the power to discipline and to punish, and it would also have to produce evidence that Kole was a party to any such terms of employment. It's the degree of influence that matters in this case, because what the Prosecution's case is, as I understand it, is that he ought to have asserted his authority as the shift commander, with the power to discipline and punish, and his failure to do that is evidence that he was encouraging, acquiescing, and condoning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sir Ivan, please bear in mind I think the time allotted of 45 minutes, which should be up now at a quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Do I get any injury time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I've taken account of that. Perhaps five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Then perhaps in those circumstances, I will conclude what I have to say about the beating with this observation: that against all of this, in my respectful submission, unsatisfactory evidence that Kole was a willing participant in anybody's beating, there is the mass of evidence that Kole did all he could to help detainees, which we've set out in the written submission at page 3(H), and all the Prosecution are saying is that he did not do enough; he could have done more. And that's what their whole case on counts 3, 4, and 5 comes down to: Yes, he did a lot, but he could have done more. In Schindler's List, Oskar Schindler, having saved the lives of hundreds, if not thousands, of Jews, breaks down in tears at the end, and says, "I could have done more." Would anyone think that because he could have done more, he ought to be prosecuted for what he didn't do? One only has to state that to disclose the absurdity, in my respectful submission, of that. Finally, can I come on to counts 6 and 7. We submit that there is no evidence whatsoever that Kole was a willing party to the killing, and that is a matter so fundamental that it's four-square behind Kordic and the Kunarac principle. They base their accusation in opening, which you can see at page 5036 onwards, on a number of allegations: At page 504, lines 2 to 3, that Kole was present when the machine-gun nests were set up outside Room 3, but no witness said that. Witnesses said that the desk was placed with sandbags and a machine-gun three, four, or five days before the shooting by guards. That was G, at page 1771, lines 8 to 17, and page 1780, lines 19 to 22. That the machine-gun gun and generator were put on the tables during Fustar's shift, not Kole's shift. That was Witness A at page 639, lines 5 to 12. "Earlier in the afternoon, that is, not on Kole's shift, I saw the machine-gun on the table. It had already been placed there," said Zubovic at page 2580, lines 10 to 18, and page 2662, lines 23, to 2663, line 4. R didn't see the machine-gun facing Room 3 between the arrival on the 20th of July and the 24th of July. S said he didn't see who placed the machine-gun there on -- or see it brought out, but it wasn't there before the soldiers arrived, so it was reasonable to conclude that they had brought it. That's at page 3627, lines 5 to 22. So so much for that major allegation made in opening by the Prosecution, not borne out by the evidence. The second was that Kole ordered the soldiers to form a semi-circle at a certain place in front of Room 3. I haven't got -- that was at page 504, line 3 to 5. I haven't got time to go through the evidence of Witness C, but it's at page 921, line 20, to 924, line 15, and at page 1009, at line 4, to 1010, at line 20, on which I observe that that is not quite what the witness said. The witness appears to be implying that Kole was trying to stop something happening, not starting it. And the third allegation made in opening, at page 504, lines 5 to 6: "A witness will say that Kole said, 'Do not shoot at the other rooms. It is well known where to shoot.'" That's at page 504, lines 5 to 6. But no witness said that in evidence, and the evidence is as set out in appendix A at 3. And if I can just add to the references at 3, please. At page 642, line 20, to 643, line 9; page 644, line 6 to 8; 687, line 3, to 688, line 20; and page 732, line 18, to 733, line 5. And we say that the Prosecution admitted, if you read the opening, that there might be some difficulty about the evidence on the Room 3 massacre against Kole, but if those four pieces of evidence had emerged, then it would be easier; they haven't emerged, and it must be even more difficult, because if the witnesses didn't say that, then there is no evidence on fundamental questions within the Kordic-Kunarac principles, and I invite the Chamber's attention to the evidence which we have analysed at page 8, paragraph 4, of the written submission. In order for there to be evidence which would enable the Tribunal to convict of counts concerning this allegation, it's not enough to say he could have been encouraging the soldiers to fire at Room 3, because they carried on firing at Room 3. One witness said it stopped. That's by the way. You would have to require, would you not, some words of positive encouragement to fire at Room 3? Which is what you were promised but which no witness said happened. And may I refer the Tribunal, the Chamber, to Witness P at pages 3230, lines 13 to 16; at page 3231, line 16, to 3232, line 8; Witness M at page 2806, lines 25, to 2807, line 3; and Witness A at page 734, lines 6 to 18. There is no evidence that Kole had any animus against the Room 3 detainees and substantial evidence to the contrary. And there is another reasonable explanation for Kole saying, "Do not fire at Rooms 1, or 1 and 2, or 1, 2, 4, or 2, 4"; namely damage limitation. You're asked by the Prosecution to infer in circumstances where in our respectful submission you cannot infer guilt, but you are capable, as a Tribunal, of using your own knowledge and experience of the world to see that if the guns had already shot at Room 3 and done the terrible damage, it's not necessarily consistent with guilt or encouragement that he says, "For goodness sake, don't shoot at any other room." Perhaps even giving desperate reasons why they shouldn't: "They are good people. They have already been interrogated. They are from Prijedor." Anything. Witness V actually said, "If he hadn't said that, all of us would be dead." That's at page 3862, line 8, to 3863, line 2. And if that is what reasonably may have been happening - and it's consistent with all the other evidence in this case, as far as Kole is concerned, once you've removed the four or five positive references that you were led to expect and didn't happen, or if they did happen you weren't reminded about the cross-examination which showed they didn't happen in the end - that would be far short of the encouragement which the Prosecution have to prove. And what it comes down to, if you look at the Prosecution's response at page 7, paragraph 13 onwards, is that all they are now saying about Kole and the Room 3 massacre is that by inference, you can say he acquiesced. And in my respectful submission, on this evidence, is that anywhere near enough to prove complicity in murder when there is so much evidence that he tried to stop the shooting? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. The overwhelming evidence about his good behaviour in the massacre is set out at page 8, paragraph 4, of our motion: Soldiers -- in our motion. Soldiers -- and also the fact in paragraph 4 is that soldiers in large numbers swept into the camp, set up a machine-gun nest, ignored all attempts by Kole to stop the shooting, and there is no evidence that Kole had any control over the army outside the camp. They came in with red ribbon on their arms, they undoubtedly did the shooting, says the evidence. And even if he might have had any control over the camp up until that moment, that control went. And Witness S, at page 3682, lines 3 to 16, says, "It did not appear that he was in a position to give any orders." Because I asked. He said, "Yes, I did say that." And did you mean by that that any control he had he had lost? One could say that. So the soldiers had taken control by then? I don't know. Well, he'd lost control, yes, if he'd ever had it? Kole, yes, you could say that. Who then had control, in your opinion? Well, at that time, those soldiers there, as likely as not. And that is the common sense of the situation. In all those circumstances, how can it be possible to say at any level of some evidence or reasonable doubt evidence, that Kole was both a participator in the shooting and that he had the evil mind necessary to do so? How can it be said that, on this evidence, there is sufficient evidence? So in conclusion, we submit the matters raised in our submission are not adequately answered by the Prosecution's response. Our submissions go to matters which are so fundamental - identification in particular, any evidence at all of willingness to participate or even evidence of actual participation himself - as to amount to the collapse of the Prosecution's case against Kole, four-square within the principle of Kordic-Kunarac, to be dealt with, we submit, now under 98 bis because sufficiency of evidence at that level is for you and for the Chamber to say that there is no case to answer on any of those counts against Kolundzija. And on behalf of Mr. Ostojic and myself, I say thank you to the Tribunal for bearing with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Sir Ivan. Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Before my learned friend addresses you, he and I have had a conversation about one matter which I think will assist you. It's in relation to torture. I raised with him the other counts of torture in the indictment, and those are 18, 19, 29, 30, 33, 34, 39 and 40. I understand from my conversation with him that he will make a similar concession in respect of those counts as well as to the concession which has been made with respect to 12 and 13. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Prior to beginning, if I could get a clarification from the Chamber with respect to the length of time we will be sitting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You must have your 45 minutes, which will take us to quarter past 1.00. Then we had allotted five minutes for each defendant to respond. The interpreters had very kindly agreed to stay with us until quarter past 1.00. I'm not certain whether they will be able to bear with us for another 15 minutes, which would take us to half past 1.00. In that case, then, we could adjourn at half past 1.00. I'm seeking the understanding of the interpreters. And then we would resume at 3.00 for the oral ruling on the submission. I haven't heard any dissent from the interpreters. So once again, on behalf of the Chamber, I'd like to thank them very much for their understanding. Please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution intends to proceed in the following manner: I will address with the Chamber with respect to some general issues that have been raised very briefly, then I will deal with the issues raised by counsel for Mr. Sikirica with respect to the genocide charges and the genocide and complicity to commit genocide counts, and then my colleague Ms. Baly will take to the floor to address the issues raised by counsel for Mr. Kolundzija and counsel for Mr. Dosen. With respect to the standard that's applicable for Rule 98 bis, I'm certainly not going to rehash that issue. The Prosecution will rely on its submissions in the written submissions. The Prosecution is quite comfortable with the -- with either the Kordic or the Kunarac standard and doesn't necessarily see that there is a contradiction between those two, as we've set forth on pages 2 to 3 of our response. With respect to cumulative charging, that issue has also been raised, and the Prosecution respectfully submits that this is not the proper time to force the Prosecution to elect between cumulative or alternative counts. In support of that, we direct -- respectfully point to the Trial Chamber's attention the decision of 15 December 2000 by the Trial Chamber I in the Kvocka and others, the Omarska case, where they quite clearly stated that issues of cumulative charging are best decided at the end of the case. And finally, we've heard several submissions this morning with respect to the opening statement that Mr. Ryneveld gave on March 19th. Of course, as the Trial Chamber is well aware, a counsel's opening statement is certainly not a matter of evidence, and the Prosecution would simply point that out for the benefit of the Chamber. Moving on now to the genocide counts, count 1 and complicity to commit genocide, count 2, very briefly, the Prosecution submits that there are in fact only two elements that must be proven to establish genocide. That is the material element of the offence, or the actus reus, and the mens rea, or the special intent element, which consists of the intention to destroy in whole or in part a national, ethnical, racial or religious group as such. With respect to the actus reus, the Prosecution has provided examples of what we are relying on in paragraphs 4, 5 and 6 of our response. Those -- the evidence cited there specifically refers back to the allegations with respect to Article 4(2)(A), (B) and (C) of the statute. I'm not intending on focusing my comments this afternoon on the actus reus. We will rely on our written submissions in those paragraphs to establish those elements at this point in time. Article 4 of the statute requires the accused Sikirica committed the genocidal acts with the intent that I have just indicated. The Prosecution contends that there are four subcomponents of this mens rea requirement: The first being the quality or degree of the intent required; the second being that it is the group as such that is to be protected under Article 4; the third is the scope of the national, ethnical, racial --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The scope of the national, ethnical, racial or religious group; and the fourth subcomponent being the destruction in whole or in part. And what I am intending on doing is dealing with the three subcomponents consisting of the proof of the special intent, the group as such, and the scope of the group. With respect to the intent requirement, the Prosecution submits that it is extremely unlikely that there will be direct evidence in any given case of an accused's intent to commit genocide. And the Appeals Chamber, the ICTR Appeals Chamber, in Kayeshima and Ruzindana, the appeal which was rendered on the 1st of June of this year, very specifically addressed that point. And in their oral summary of the judgement, the ICTR Appeals Chamber stated: "Regarding a lack of explicit manifestation of intent, the Appeals Chamber is of the view that the requisite intent may normally be inferred from facts and circumstances." They went on to say: "Generally, such an intent may be inferred from the words or deeds of the perpetrator and may be demonstrated by a pattern of conduct, a deliberate pattern of conduct." The Appeals Chamber, the ICTR Appeals Chamber, however, went on to state that this persistent pattern of conduct was not an element of the crime of genocide but rather a means of proof so as to demonstrate whether the accused actually possessed the requisite intent. As we set forth in our written submissions, the Prosecution in the Jelesic appeal, set forth seven factors which may be probative of -- or may lead to inferences demonstrating the intent; and again, those seven factors are set forth in the written submissions. I'm intending now to lead you through each of those seven factors and point you in the evidence which in the Prosecution's respectful submission demonstrates or would lead a reasonable Trial Chamber to draw the inference with respect to the intent issue. The first of these issues is the general and widespread nature of the atrocities committed, and in a sense, this element or this component, if you will, is similar to the widespread or systematic element with respect to crimes against humanity under Article 5. However, the Prosecution asserts that it is not again an element of genocide but simply a means of proving the intent through the use of an inference. And in this case, the Prosecution has adduced a great deal of evidence concerning the general and widespread nature of the atrocities committed throughout opstina Prijedor during the relevant time periods as indicated in the indictment. The following communities were particularly hard hit by the Serb campaign, to include: Kozarac, Hambarine, Ljubija, Brdo, Cvici, Trnopolje, Puharska, Tukovi, Crkvica, Rakovcani and Rizvanovici. The testimony also of Witness A, at pages 702 and 703 of the transcript, are particularly helpful in this respect. As you will recall, Witness A was one of the original or one of the very first individuals detained in Keraterm, and as such, he recalled during the course of his testimony the locations from which subsequent detainees were arriving from, and so he actually was able to provide the Chamber with, in effect, a list, an ongoing list, of the areas that had been ethnically cleansed as these individuals were brought into the camp. Similarly, other witnesses, including Witness D, at pages 1048 and 1049, spoke about refugees fleeing into the Ljubija area, again demonstrating the very widespread and general nature of the atrocities committed. With respect to the second element, the general political doctrine giving rise to the acts, the Prosecution will draw to the attention of the Trial Chamber the Appeals Chamber ruling in the Tadic case, and particularly paragraphs 230 and 234 of the Appeals Chamber decision whereby the Appeals Chamber affirmed the Tadic Trial Chamber opinion, and specifically paragraph 660 of that opinion, and stated that - again, the Appeals Chamber: "The Trial Chamber found that the appellant" - again in that case, Dusko Tadic - "participated in the armed conflict taking place between May and December 1992 in the Prijedor region. An aspect of this conflict was a policy to commit inhumane acts against the non-Serb civilian population of the territory in the attempt to achieve the creation of a greater Serbia." The Prosecution will submit that that finding by the Appeals Chamber certainly can be a component of drawing the inference with respect to the accused's intent. The scale of the actual or attempted destruction is the third component, and in this respect the Prosecution specifically draws to the attention of the Trial Chamber three documents that have been introduced into evidence, and at this point, we simply indicate that, as of yet, the Prosecution has not been notified by the Registry as to the official exhibit numbers of these documents, so I will simply refer to them by the numbers that the Prosecution had affixed to these documents at the time they were provided and filed. The first one being the report of the expert demographer, Uwe Tabo [phoen], which the Prosecution filed on 23 April, 2001. This report clearly demonstrates that the population of Bosnian Muslims in Prijedor decreased dramatically between 1991 and 1993. In 1991, the opstina had 49.351 Muslims. By 1993, there were 6.124 Muslims, a decrease of 87.6 per cent. During the same time period, the population of Serbs living in Prijedor increased, not just as a percentage of the overall population, as one would expect with such a dramatic decrease in the number of Muslims in the opstina, but in terms of actual numbers as well. In 1991, 47.581 Serbs lived in Prijedor, in 1993, 53.637 Serbs were living there, an increase of 12.7 per cent. Documents numbered 9.16 and 9.17 demonstrate, in the Prosecution's respectful view, that officials in Banja Luka, the self-styled capital of Republika Srpska, took an active interest in the census data, requiring the Prijedor officials to provide them with precise and current census data. The fourth component deals with the methodical way of planning the killings, and the Prosecution submits that there is proof of several examples which would lead the Trial Chamber to draw the necessary inference with respect to the accused's intent. Let's take the Room 3 massacre and the preparations for that, as an example. Room 3 was prepared for the Brdo area men through a process of emptying the room of its detainees. Witness A, pages 619 and 620. Machine-gun nests were set up outside of the room. Again, transcript pages 891, 921 through 923; pages 1594, pages 974 to 976; and importantly from the Prosecution's view, pages 2580 and 2662, which indicate that those machine-gun nests were placed in the afternoon during the time which other witnesses have testified was the time that normally Mr. Sikirica was in the camp. We had testimony that searchlights were set up outside of the room in anticipation of the night-time attack on that room. There was testimony that tear gas was thrown into the room in order to incapacitate and disorient the detainees. In the Prosecution's view, that was also done in an attempt to force those individuals in that room to flee that room, thereby giving the attackers the excuse that the detainees in that room were trying to escape. And finally, we had several witnesses, including Witness L at page 2509 and Witness C at page 818, testify about additional soldiers and guards being brought into the camp on the evening of the massacre. The systematic manner of killing and disposal of the bodies. Again in this instance, the Prosecution would submit that the testimony of Witness M at pages 2710 through 2711, and Witness Q at 3251 and 3252, are particularly relevant with respect to the genocidal acts as alleged in the indictment. Finally in this respect, the Prosecution would point out that there was a typographical error in the Prosecution's response with respect to the accused Mr. Sikirica, specifically footnote 12 on page 4, wherein we cited to Witness S in support of the proposition that the accused Sikirica personally shot 18 to 20 Room 3 survivors on the morning after the massacre. The actual support --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The actual support for this proposition may be found on pages 2710 through 2711, and 3251 through 3252, during the testimony of Witness M and Witness Q respectively. The Prosecution, in addition, submits that the methodical and systematic disposal of the bodies certainly could lead to an inference with respect to intent. And in that respect, the testimony of numerous witnesses concerning the loading of bodies onto a truck following the massacre as well as the disposal of the bodies at the Pasinac cemetery --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, all the factors that you've identified, the several of them, would be just as consistent, would they not be, with persecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. They would certainly demonstrate an intent to commit persecution as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The difficulty, as I see it, that you have is to establish this very special, this very specific, intent, which is set out in Article 4, and we have to be careful not to confuse genocide with other criminal conduct covered under Article 5, such as persecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Absolutely. The Prosecution would certainly agree with the position that Your Honour has stated, and let me respond in two ways. First of all, we also have the evidence of what the Prosecution has submitted constitute the genocidal acts, which are the personal acts that the accused committed, which again, in anticipation of a question from the Bench, could also be evidence of murder as acts of persecution, but more specifically - and that would be the next area that I am hoping to address in my relatively limited amount of time - would go to the establishment or, if you will, how to conceptualise the group that the Prosecution alleged was the collective victim of this -- of these genocidal acts. And perhaps if I can get to that and perhaps that will address the questions that Your Honour has. Let me move right to that, in light of the time constraints. Article 4 imposes an obligation on the Prosecution to identify the members of the group based on very specific characteristics, including national, ethnical, religious or racial grounds. In this case, the group is characterised by its religion, being Islam. Once the group has been identified, however, it's necessary to consider the scope or the size of the group that the Prosecution alleges is being targeted. There certainly is no evidence in this case, nor is there any evidence from which the Trial Chamber could infer, that the intent of the accused Sikirica was to destroy the Bosnian Muslims in total. The Prosecution will acknowledge that. However, in this case, the Prosecution has alleged, and our Pre-Trial brief deals with this extensively, that the group in question, the scope of the group in question, is the leadership of the Bosnian Muslim community in opstina Prijedor. The next question, then, becomes, was the intent to destroy that group in whole or in part? Again, the Prosecution position with respect to this targeted group is that the accused had the intent to destroy that group, i.e., the leadership, and the leadership would include those individuals who most actively resisted the Serb takeover, to include the Room 3 individuals. That group being the targeted group, the Prosecution position is that the accused had the intent to destroy that group in part. Now, this -- this group, if you will, the evidence that we have of other -- of people who constituted this group, again would be those who most actively resisted the Serb takeover, to include the individuals from the Brdo area, as the evidence has been adduced that that area was one of the last pockets of resistance to the Serb military takeover in Prijedor. However, there were also religious leaders who were targeted. There were educators who were targeted. Witness A, Fikret Hidic, and Witness X have all talked about teachers being subjected to particularly violent behaviour. Lawyers were singled out, as Witness C testified. Several witnesses talked about police officers being specifically targeted. And Witness I, at page 2088, and Witness E at page 1291, talked of wealthy individuals or business leaders who were specifically targeted. The Prosecution further contends that by targeting this group, this group of community leaders, in light of what else had been happening in opstina Prijedor, that is, the overall general context of what had been happening, this was particularly devastating to the Bosnian Muslim community as a whole; that by targeting its leadership, this was an integral part of the overall campaign, if you will, of ethnically cleansing Prijedor of its Bosnian Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, I'm concerned about your definition of leadership as including, it seems to me, every person who resisted the takeover. You include in your concept of leadership not just those who would traditionally be considered leaders - doctors, lawyers, businessmen, and so on - but you say every person who resisted, and by that reasoning you would include all those who were from Brdo and in Room 3; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I mischaracterised what we were intending to rely upon as the leaders. Certainly it would include, as Your Honour has pointed out, the doctors, the lawyers, the business leaders, the police officers. But with respect to those people who resisted in the Brdo area, the Prosecution would contend that they are analogous, if you will, for this purpose, to military leaders, that these are -- that, in effect, because of their active resistance, they were an example to other smaller communities, not only in Prijedor, perhaps, but in the larger region as a whole; that, in effect, they were targeted because they assumed this leadership role, and that group could include individuals who would not necessarily be otherwise considered leaders but for the fact that they actively resisted; and by assuming that position of being active participants in resisting the Serb military takeover, the Prosecution contends that they in effect became leaders, leaders of the greater Bosnian Muslim community, if you will, or they were serving as examples, and it was partially for that reason that they were then targeted, as in their role as leaders they were targeted. I hope that clarifies the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, very briefly, I just want to hit on several submissions of the accused -- counsel for the accused Sikirica. First of all, in their written submissions, they contended that the Prosecution had failed to establish that there was, in fact, a genocide in Prijedor. And the Prosecution position on this is very clear, and it stems from the Jelisic Trial Chamber decision that there is no requirement that we prove a genocide occurred in Prijedor. There is the requirement that we prove genocidal acts were committed and we prove that the accused had the requisite mens rea. That is all we need to prove with respect to genocide. Similarly, counsel for the accused Sikirica has alleged that we have failed to prove that there was a campaign to commit genocide, and in that respect, again the Prosecution submits that there is no requirement of proof of an overall objective context in which that genocide takes place. We have addressed that in the Pre-Trial brief, and specifically, I would draw to the Trial Chamber's attention paragraphs 148 to 154, where we discuss that at greater length. Noting the time, Your Honour, unless there are any further questions, I feel I must yield to my colleague, Ms. Baly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Ms. Baly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I feel somewhat under siege, but I will do my best to finish by a quarter past 1.00. Dealing firstly with the submissions made by Mr. Petrovic on behalf of Mr. Dosen this morning, Mr. Petrovic named one individual as an individual who was on the list in his written motion and for whom the Prosecution, in his submission, did not lead any evidence whatsoever. Your Honours, Mr. Petrovic is quite correct, and it was an omission on my part insofar the written document is concerned. That individual was simply overlooked, and it is conceded that there is no evidence in relation to that individual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's Agan -- do you have the name?

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: It's the person Duratovic, Your Honour, in confidential attachment A, the one individual that was named by Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. We'll find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: In relation to the other individuals named, they are dealt with at paragraph 5 of the written response. The names, in the submission -- in my submission, in the submission of the Prosecution, fall into two categories: Firstly, A to I, the names of individuals for whom there is evidence that they were found in a mass grave, and independent evidence that they were -- these particular individuals were in fact in Keraterm. The second category concerns individuals I to P. For those individuals, the Prosecution relies upon evidence that they were found in a mass grave together with other individuals for whom there is independent evidence that the other individuals were in fact in Keraterm. And the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you say A to I and then I to P?

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: I to P.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: A to I. Then the next list would be J to P; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, Your Honour. That's correct. Generally turning to the evidence against Damir Dosen: In the submission of the Prosecution, there is overwhelming evidence that acts of persecution took place within the camp. And I'm addressing entirely the camp persecution, having regard to the acknowledgment made in the written submission in relation to the counts 12 to 15 in the indictment. There is abundant evidence that the accused was a shift commander at Keraterm detention camp. Without exception, the witnesses who were in the camp were able to discern a distinct hierarchy in terms of the personnel who guarded them, placing the accused as second only to the commander of the camp and with direct supervision over at least ten guards on his shift. Contrary to the evidence -- to the submission made by my learned friend, there is abundant evidence that he had authority within the camp such that at times he did, in fact, alter the conditions. It flows from that that at other times he could also alter the conditions. It's submitted by the Prosecution that his authority arises not only from his de jure position as commander but also his de facto actions. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Insofar as liability is concerned under 7(1), Article 7(1), it arises in a number of capacities: firstly, directly via acts of persecution that witnesses said the accused committed himself. Those are cited -- examples of those are cited in the written submissions. And in the same category, his presence in the camp when acts of persecution were taking place during his shift, and indirectly via his participation in a common purpose, and in that sense the common purpose relied upon could be any one of the categories as articulated in the decision of Tadic. It's submitted that the accused's participation in that common purpose arises -- can be inferred from three distinct categories of evidence: Firstly, from his position as the shift commander; secondly, from his actions within the camp; and thirdly, from statements from his own mouth. In that respect, I just want to cite one quote. I'd invite Your Honours to look at page 3462 of the transcript, together with page 2585 of the transcript, which is not referred to in the written submission, so I will read it to the Court. And it says this, commencing at line 1: "One morning" -- and this is witness Zubovic, in open session: "One morning, just before Kajin was to take over duty, between 5.00 and 6.00 he appeared at the door of dormitory 3. He was clearly drunk and he addressed the detainees. But as far as one could learn from what he said, he was addressing the detainees he knew from before. And he said how he was sorry for everything that was happening --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you slow down, please, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... the men he knew.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel, will you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Serbs had suffered during the Second World War, that now it was our turn to suffer; that he didn't find everything that happened easy, but what astonished me was his explicit statement that what happened in Room 3 had to happen because inside were extremists exclusively, and what happened to them was something that they had deserved, in his words. From those three categories of evidence, Your Honours could infer that he was a part of common purpose, and that common purpose included his knowledge of what was going on in other camps, including the Omarska camp, and there are several references to his statements insofar as Omarska is concerned in the written pleadings. The same evidence is relied upon to found liability on the part of the accused Damir Dosen insofar as Article 7(3) is concerned. In the remaining time, turning to the accused Dragan Kolundzija, let me first make two very brief observations regarding my learned friend's submissions under 98 bis insofar as the standard is concerned. Just two brief points. The distinction is, in my submission, encapsulated in the phrase that the Trial Chamber at the 98 bis stage is considering whether it could convict as opposed to whether it would convict; and secondly, as to questions of credit, which include questions of reliability and include questions of reliability in an identification case, the Prosecution maintains that it's generally not a matter to be considered but accepts that where it can be said that the Prosecution case has completely broken down, the Court is entitled to consider questions of credibility, which include reliability. Turning to the evidence against the accused Kolundzija, dealing firstly with accounts of persecution, there again is abundant evidence that acts of persecution did in fact take place. There is again abundant evidence that the accused was a shift leader in the camp. My learned friend has submitted that there is an absence of evidence of his formal powers and his formal capacity. The evidence in this matter arises not only from his de jure position as a shift commander, but also his de facto actions and ability to alter the conditions, as demonstrated by him, which the Prosecution says he did so discriminately. He did good things for some prisoners; he didn't do as much as he could in the circumstances. There is also evidence that the accused was more directly involved in persecutory acts within the camp. And again, those witnesses upon whom the Prosecution rely are listed in the written pleadings, and they are Witness N, Witness O, Witness X, Jusuf Arifagic, and Witness P. Just one point in relation to the Room 3 massacre: The prisoners who were subject to that massacre were, it is submitted, treated inhumanely by -- during all shifts, including that of Kole's, and it is to be remembered that it was the accused himself who organised for Room 3 to be vacated so that those prisoners could be segregated and indeed treated particularly inhumanely. In relation to Witness O, just one point, and that is: She is able in her testimony, when Your Honours read the entire testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You don't have much time. You say that Kole organised for the room to be segregated so that they could be treated particularly inhumanely.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. He organised for the -- there is evidence that he called the chiefs of the rooms together and asked them to make way in their respective rooms for the prisoners who were then housed, that is, prior to the arrival of the Brdo prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: When Your Honours read the entirety of the evidence of Witness O, yes, she does say that she left when she was asked to or told to by the accused. However, she is able, when she is standing there with the accused, to witness what was happening to those prisoners as they exited the bus. That is, she witnessed -- she describes the uniforms of the perpetrators, she describes the nature of the beating that they received as they left the bus. Now, the only inference to be drawn from that is that she was there for some time, time enough to witness the event. During the time she was there, the accused did nothing. Turning, in the next couple of minutes, to the Room 3 massacre which founds liability on the part of the accused under counts 6 and 7 of the indictment, that of murder, there is certainly, and it is conceded, a large body of evidence that a large number of detainees were killed and were killed wilfully. There is a considerable body of evidence that this was a planned event. These prisoners were treated differently, particularly inhumanely, from their arrival in the camp; again, even on Kole's shift. There is substantial evidence of the preparation for the massacre, including the setting up of the machine-gun and the table, the searchlights, extra personnel, and it's to be -- it's important to take into account the fact that Kole was on duty at 6.00 p.m. that night. The evidence is that the shooting didn't commence until around midnight. There was six hours. It certainly must have been reasonably foreseeable on his part that the Room 3 prisoners were going to be fired upon, in the submission of the Prosecution. It is important, in the Prosecution's submission, to view the words attributed to the accused on that night during the massacre in the context of the fact that these prisoners had been particularly badly treated and in view and against the background of the preparations that had been made for this massacre. When viewed against that background, there is one striking consistency in terms of the words that the prisoners -- the detainees recalled, and that is: Don't shoot at whatever rooms, at Rooms 1, 2, 4, but no mention of not shooting toward Room 3. Witness C is an important witness in this regard because Witness C says that what he heard was the words, "Don't do it without my order," and he says he heard those words before any firing commenced. It's quite feasible in the circumstances that the accused was saying different things at various times. But if you take those words and you place it against the context and the background and the fact that the accused commenced duty at 6.00 p.m. that evening, in the circumstances, there is an inference available that he was indeed acquiescing in the killing of the so-called extremists in Room 3. Finally, just two points in relation to matters raised by my learned friend. Firstly, Mr. Edward Vulliamy was not in the position of the accused, so it's not surprising he didn't know what was going on in other camps. It would be indeed astonishing if the accused did not. And secondly, Oskar Schindler was not a shift commander in a detention camp where one ethnic group incarcerated and brutally abused another. Those are my submissions. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Baly. Mr. Greaves, five minutes, which you're not obliged to use.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I can forgive Your Honour for trying on each occasion. Your Honour, my learned friend Mr. Mundis said that the Pre-Trial brief and the Prosecution opening are not matters of evidence. That, of course, is right. But then, of course, he then proceeded to rely on his own document in much the same way as Defence counsel had done. What is sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander. The second matter: He relied on the -- effectively, as I understood it, the summary of the Kayeshima judgement that was handed out at the time. Could I commend Your Honours actually reading paragraph 93, which I think is slightly different in terms from the way in which he put it. In particular, can I draw Your Honours' attention to the references there to the issue of the numbers of victims from the group being important in assessing when you're looking at inferential evidence. What we have in this case is, in terms of Keraterm, 1500 people being detained and perhaps 300 or so being killed. In the context of the total number of people in Prijedor, the total number of Muslims, that is a tiny proportion. Reference was made to the general and widespread nature of the atrocities committed. I repeat: But it is important that there is no evidence in this case that the defendant was aware of what was taking place. My learned friend relied on the case of Tadic and the evidence in that case that Tadic took part in armed conflict. There is a great distinction here in this case, because there is no evidence that Dusko Sikirica took part in armed conflict. His participation in these matters is limited to events at Keraterm, and in that sense it is quite different from the case of Tadic. Tadic could no doubt have concluded from what he did and what he saw during the course of the armed conflict all sorts of things. There is not a shred of evidence in this case that Dusko Sikirica was out in the field other than being at the checkpoint at Hambarine, which, of course, has a very limited horizon. My learned friend relied on the census. Of course, those are raw pieces of statistics. What it doesn't, of course -- no doubt in the period immediately after armed conflict, there are a number of people who leave. Some may leave because they are persecuted. Others may leave, as happens in wars all over the world, because they flee fighting, because they are afraid that they may be caught in the crossfire, and that is plainly what happened. That statistic is a statistic, and no more and no less than that. I turn now to the point that Your Honour raised, and, if I may respectfully submit, a good point. That is that these facts which are relied on and those factors which are relied upon by the Prosecution are equally indicative of the existence of persecution as they are of genocide, and Your Honour referred to the rather higher standard that one has to achieve in order to prove the intent for genocide. In our submission, Your Honour has put your finger exactly on the point. All those factors are equally redolent of persecution as they are of genocide, and if they could be one or the other, then the task which I submit you have to do, the exercise you have to do, is to say this: If they are equally consistent with one or the other, then we must conclude that they are, in the favour of the defendant, proof of persecution rather than proof of genocide. My learned friend then went on to deal with one aspect of what he called the targeting in this case, and that is of the leadership. Your Honour, what in essence the Prosecution are saying, we submit, is that a political group was being targeted. We submit that political groups fall without the genocide convention, and if a political group is being targeted -- and there was great discussion at the time of the coming into force of the treaty concerning genocide, concerning political groups who were considered but specifically rejected from protection, and we say that if the Prosecution are trying to extend the law, then it should not be done. Secondly, in relation to that aspect, there is no evidence that Dusko Sikirica knew in any way or could have had information from which he could infer that throughout the area of the Prijedor opstina, it was the leadership which was in fact being targeted during the course of these events. My learned friend then also relied on the case of Jelisic in a -- what I would respectfully submit was an entirely selective way. One should, of course, remember that the Prosecution has impugned the Jelisic judgement in its appeal. One wonders how they feel able, with a straight face, to rely on that judgement in this Court, having impugned that judgement. I mention the matter because in that case, as I recall it, one of the elements that the learned Judges said was necessary for proof of genocide was the existence of a plan, something which the Prosecution doesn't rely on in this case. One should view their reliance on Jelisic in that way as a somewhat flawed exercise. Finally this: There is no evidence that Dusko Sikirica was present during any of the Room 3 massacre at all. That is a matter which is important if one is considering the inferential side of matters, and we would draw that particularly to your attention. And my final observation which I'm asked to remind you, that there is no evidence at all of a positive kind concerning the special intention in respect of genocide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Greaves. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all, in connection with what my learned friend opposite said regarding the general points of the indictment in relation to my client, persecution, and this relates to counts 12 to 15. I think she made a mistake, that she is really referring to counts 3 to 5, on the basis of the Prosecution response, as counts 12 to 15 relate precisely to what I referred to, that is, an event which did not occur and which the Prosecution has conceded in its response. So I think this is an error and nothing more, and that the Prosecution is not changing its position as expressed in their response to our motion of the 8th of June. That is the first point I should like to make. Second, also very briefly, in connection with what my learned friend opposite said, that is, the alleged awareness of Damir Dosen of what was happening, which he himself said when he was in front of a certain room. To be quite precise, I wish to underline - and this may have been said by omission - this was not happening in front of Room 3, as was stated a moment ago in the oral submission of my learned friend, but in front of Room 2. And in reference to Hajrudin Zubovic, this is also in the transcript, so I think that was another error. Also, there is a wide variety of different interpretations of the situation which differ significantly from what the Prosecution is telling us in an attempt to prove that Dosen had knowledge as to what was happening in Keraterm and beyond, within the municipality of Prijedor. Finally, I should like to appeal to Your Honours: If there is anything in connection with the nature of these facts that could be admitted and was mentioned by Mr. Greaves and Sir Ivan, that your decision should embrace my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Sir Ivan -- Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may address the Court. Thank you. May it please the Court, I have two actual areas to submit. First, generally: The Office of the Prosecutor, as this panel knows, has five specific counts against Dragan Kolundzija. Within each count, they allege various articles: Article 7(1), Article 7(3), Article 5, and Article 3. With respect, and I submit to this panel respectfully, when you examine each of the counts, you should examine 7(1), and you'll find that the Office of the Prosecutor, not only in their submission but in their oral comments today, have conceded counts 4 and 5 insofar as that there's no evidence presented to substantiate a verdict under any standard against Dragan Kolundzija. Specifically with respect to section 7(1), direct responsibility, we submit that the evidence has been overwhelmingly and unequivocally in favour of Mr. Kolundzija insofar as that he did not, at any time during the period involving this indictment at Keraterm camp, directly or, as the case may be, indirectly participate in any inhumane treatments, outrages of personal dignity, or persecution to any of the detainees. With respect to all of the five counts, we would request that this panel acquit Mr. Kolundzija vis-a-vis 7(1). With respect to 7(3), command superiority, the fundamental premise of the Prosecutor - and I believe they acknowledge it implicitly, or at least by inference, to use their word - they cannot find an instance from any of the witnesses that they've presented that an act of brutality, ill-treatment, mistreatment, beating, occurred by a subordinate of Dragan Kolundzija during the time that he was present at the camp during his shift. Similarly, we would ask this Honourable Court to acquit Mr. Kolundzija of all of those five counts with respect to the theory of 7(3). The remaining counts, and particularly I'd like to address the evidence that Ms. Baly, my learned friend, has addressed, and that is Witness O. Witness O was an individual who stated that she saw, on July 20, 1992, when the bus arrived at Keraterm camp, that some or at least one of the detainees that was brought there being beaten. At that point, she was approximately 50 metres away. What the Prosecution is really telling you, I suggest, is that they're asking for seconds, if not less time, for the defendant, the accused in this case, Dragan Kolundzija, to have reacted to that instantaneous and spontaneous beating that had occurred. We submit that it's illogical and unreasonable for the Prosecution to rest their entire case on those milliseconds from the time when Witness O was present and perceives to have seen something and when action would be required by Mr. Kolundzija. The inhumane treatment, as the Prosecution suggests occurred on all the shifts, is entirely too vague for this Court to attribute any responsibility to Dragan Kolundzija. It's vague because Mr. Kolundzija had acted, as all the witnesses have said - even the witness that they rely on particularly, Witness C - that he had saved them and that everything possible in order to make --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will. Sorry. To make their time at the camp reasonable and better. He, in fact, enhanced some of the conditions, as in Room 3 particularly. For example, Witness R and Witness P respectfully have said that the detainees in Room 3 were permitted during Dragan Kolundzija's shift to exit the room so that they can have an opportunity to obtain fresh air and breathe. And also, they unlocked the door so they can have an opportunity to walk around in the pista, as this panel has heard. And interestingly enough, one of the witnesses also, as this Court will recall, stated that Mr. Kolundzija had a discussion and an argument in essence and fought with Mr. Sikirica about allowing the detainees in Room number 3 access outside of that room as opposed to continuously keeping them confined within that room. We submit that that evidence infers not only actions that this panel should hold actions in favour of Dragan Kolundzija, but we submit that this panel, on all five counts, should - indeed must - acquit Dragan Kolundzija for the actions that have been alleged by the Prosecutor here. Finally, I'd like to just tell this panel, if you examine not only our submission and the testimony and the standard of review that's been discussed, there has not been, in our view, one witness who, standing alone, could have unequivocally stated anything to fulfil the elements of the counts that are charged against Dragan Kolundzija. In essence, what this panel -- regardless of which standard or difference or distinction there may be of the standards, the Prosecution was unable to provide this Court with one witness who did not, under the test of cross-examination, either completely crumble or create a significant doubt, i.e., a reasonable doubt, as it relates to our client Dragan Kolundzija, and therefore we ask once again that on all five counts, including 7(1), the theory 7(3), that this panel acquit Dragan Kolundzija. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I now give the ruling on the submissions made in relation to Rule 98 bis. Firstly, the Chamber reaffirms the test set out in Kordic and Cerkez for the application of Rule 98 bis, that is, whether there is evidence on the basis of which a reasonable Tribunal could convict. It does not understand the reference in Kunarac to reasonable doubt to imply that the Trial Chamber must be satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt of the guilt of the accused in a particular case before it can refuse a submission under Rule 98 bis. Rather, the reference in Kunarac is a gloss on the meaning of "could convict" and there is no contradiction between the two decisions. On that basis, the Chamber makes the following rulings: One, the submission on behalf of Sikirica in respect of the charges of genocide and complicity to commit genocide is allowed, for the reason that the Prosecution has failed to establish the specific intent required by Article 4 of the statute, that is, to destroy in whole or in part a national, ethnical, racial or religious group as such. Two, the submission on behalf of Dosen in respect of counts 12 to 15, alleging torture, cruel treatment and inhumane acts, is allowed. In this regard, the Chamber notes the concession made by the Prosecution that the only role attributable to Dosen during the alleged incident is exculpatory in nature. The Chamber has considered the submissions made by Mr. Greaves and Mr. Mundis that by virtue of paragraphs 14 and 17 of the general allegations in the indictment, a charge under Article 7(3) of the statute would apply to Sikirica - and I might add to all the other accused - in respect of all counts of the indictment irrespective of whether the accused has been specifically charged under Article 7(3). The Chamber considers that this construction of the indictment is inconsistent with its general pattern in which a charge under Article 7(3) is always expressly and specifically mentioned. There is therefore no need to consider the application of Rule 98 bis in relation to Article 7(3), except where an accused has been specifically charged in a count thereunder. Three, the submission on behalf of Damir Dosen in respect of counts 3 to 5, charging persecutions, inhumane acts and outrages upon personal dignity, is allowed to the extent that the following names will be deleted from Attachment A: (redacted )
